- If sentiment is consistently negative (0.00 or low) over recent days, model tends to overcorrect downward; adjust forecast upward by 1–3% to avoid underestimating rebound.
- If sentiment is consistently positive (1.00 or high) and price is trending down, model often fails to anticipate reversal; add a small upward bias (e.g., +1–2%) to prevent premature bottoming.
- After sharp price spikes (e.g., >5% in 3–5 days), model frequently overestimates continuation; apply a “cool-down” rule: reduce forecast slope by 10–20% for next 5–7 days.
- When sentiment is neutral (0.5–0.67) and price is volatile, model often fails to capture mean reversion; apply a “mean-reversion” heuristic: shift forecast toward 30-day moving average of prior 10–15 days.
- If model shows steady upward trend with no sentiment signal, it often overestimates; cap forecast at 10–15% below recent high if sentiment is flat or negative.
- If sentiment turns positive after a downtrend, model often lags; add 1–2 days of “sentiment lag” to forecast, i.e., delay upward shift by 1–2 days to match sentiment momentum.
